I can't remember having seen a movie with this many entirely unnecessary sex-scenes. "The Pianist" is one of my favorite movies of all times and Adrian Brody is a magnificent actor. Unfortunately, "The Brutalist" is a boring, sometimes confusing if not erratic movie that lost me when after a sudden timeskip of unknown time in the second half Laszlow's niece Zsofia, who we only saw as a young girl that was mute from the war trauma she had experienced, all of sudden was talking like it is the most normal thing. The movie never explains what happened, why the girl suddenly gained the ability to talk again, it's just something that happened. And that's true for the entire second half of the movie: Things happen. Are they exciting? Interesting? Fun? No. But they happen. And then the credits started running. I know this is from a different director (and a heartfelt "fuck you" to rapist Roman Polanski), but it's hard not to wish for a direct sequel to "The Pianist" when seeing Adrian Brody playing the role of a post-WW2 jew. There's a lot that could have been portrayed in such sequel. Instead, we're following Lazslow who flees from Europe to America to start a new life. And that is interesting. We see how he arrives, how he struggles, how cruel this unknown world is to him. We see how he rises up, gets chances and takes them. This is when this movie is at its best. This is the fantastic first half. And then his wife arrives and the movie gets worse and worse from there. Instead of focusing on the building of the ... building and the struggles that come with such work, we only ever get a surface-level look at his work. Instead, more and more time is spent on family issues, trauma and drug abuse. And sex. Lots of sex scenes. Those are important for reasons. The final 20 minutes or so would have been the moment where I would have walked out of the theater hadn't I watched the movie at  home. Without spoiling much, "The Brutalist" pulls a "Joker: Folie a Deux" and completely torpedos everything that came before. Absolute baffeling choice. Not a movie I want to watch again and not a movie that felt like it was telling an important story. The gimmicky use of loud sound effects during certain scenes felt desperate.

Uma Bela Propaganda Ainda é Propaganda: A Perversidade do Cinema Pró-Genocídio 1. Propaganda Sionista Travestida de Cinema Uma peça de propaganda sionista travestida de cinema: assim podemos definir a experiência maçante de pouco mais de três horas que objetivam uma única mensagem: os judeus não são capazes de se assimilar a qualquer nação; portanto, sua única alternativa é a colonização da região Palestina. Essa mensagem perversa é incutida subliminarmente através de um voice-over nos primeiros 20 minutos de filme. O som que narra através das ondas do rádio a resolução que criou o Estado Genocida de Israel prepara o espectador para o inevitável caminho do povo judeu, e o filme irá trabalhar intensamente para justificar a aliá (migração dos judeus para colonizar a Palestina). 2. O Paralelo com Leni Riefenstahl Esse conteúdo já seria perverso em qualquer período histórico, mas, em tempos de um Holocausto promovido por Israel, ganha contornos semelhantes aos de O Triunfo da Vontade, de Leni Riefenstahl, com duas diferenças básicas: Leni era profundamente mais dominante em sua técnica e, naquele momento, o Holocausto judeu ainda não havia se consolidado, como o dos palestinos na atualidade. 3. A Fachada Progressista e a Supremacia Judaica O filme tenta levianamente travestir-se de progressista e anticapitalista para vender sua mensagem. Mas falha justamente em seu juízo moral e na evocação velada da supremacia judaica, afinal, como é citado pela personagem de Felicity Jones: "todos nesse país são podres". Deixando claro que não se trata de uma crítica ao sistema e sim aos gentios de modo geral. 4. Hollywood e a Tradição do Cinema Pró-Genocídio Não há novidades na relação entre o Estado de Israel e Hollywood. Aliás, isso sempre foi pauta em muitas discussões sobre a parcialidade do cinema estadunidense para com os diversos extermínios orquestrados pelo Estado Ilegítimo. Desde Exodus, de Otto Preminger, que desumaniza os árabes vítimas da Nakba, até produções mais recentes, como Setembro 5, Hollywood toma parte do opressor, assim como o cinema alemão o fez nos anos 30 e 40. 5. Méritos Técnicos e a Atuação de Adrien Brody Como pontos positivos do filme, podemos destacar a fotografia e a direção de arte, que tornam o filme um belo e ordinário exemplar de propaganda. Há também a grande atuação de Adrien Brody, vencedor do Oscar pelo longa, mas cuja extensão exagerada do filme acaba em alguns momentos saturando o espectador. 6. Conclusão: O Brilho Técnico Ofuscado pela Podridão Narrativa O Brutalista é uma perversidade envolta em erros e que tem poucos acertos em sua construção. Há o brilho técnico, porém ofuscado pela absorvente podridão narrativa e tentativa de ludibriar os olhos que veem a história ser escrita com lágrimas e sangue inocente.

For a movie made during a genocide which is being live-streamed and documented in real time, The Brutalist's framing of Israel is extremely disturbing and problematic. The Brutalist's description of America as a place where Jews will never truly be accepted, contrasted with Israel as a kind of promised land where they can finally belong, is presented with remarkably little critical distance. For a film dealing so heavily with displacement, trauma and the consequences of nationalism, framing Israel's creation primarily as a Jewish refuge without seriously acknowledging the Palestinians who were displaced and subjected to decades of violence, feels deeply problematic. This becomes even harder to overlook when viewed from our modern day perspective, amid Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza. Someone coming to this film with little knowledge of the history could easily leave with an extremely simplified picture: Jews were persecuted, Israel offered them safety, and that's essentially where the story ends. The question of what happened to the people already living there barely exists. I'm not asking the film to become an Israel/Palestine manifesto. But if you're going to invoke this history, especially while making such a grand film about trauma, displacement and power, you can't pretend the creation of Israel was fair, justified and necessary. And that's what disappointed me most. The Brutalist wants to be a film about the weight of history, but when confronted with one of its most uncomfortable consequences, it seems unwilling to carry that weight. The historical liberties bothered me too, particularly the manufactured suffering in László's backstory.  The real people László is based on neither survived a concentration camp nor struggled to rebuild their careers after WWII in the way the film depicts. Those aren't minor embellishments; they're fundamental parts of his character and story. The film essentially manufactures an entire history of suffering that its real-life inspirations didn't experience, presumably to make his struggle more profound. Instead, it feels manipulative and cheapens the entire premise. And the use of AI is almost comically at odds with a film so concerned with art, craftsmanship and authenticity. The film is beautiful visually but ultimately much less brave than it thinks it is.

“The Brutalist”, de Brady Corbet, sigue a László Tóth, arquitecto húngaro y sobreviviente del Holocausto, cuando intenta reconstruir su vida en Estados Unidos. El sueño americano pronto se convierte en una incómoda relación entre arte, dinero y poder. Corbet construye un drama de época monumental, fotografiado por Lol Crawley con una textura áspera y elegante. La puesta en escena impresiona, aunque su extensa duración y cambios de género terminan dispersando el relato. La película habla de migración, pertenencia, explotación y del precio de perseguir una idea. Sin embargo, su discurso sobre el sionismo resulta problemático, especialmente por una mirada que presenta Israel como único refugio seguro para los judíos. A eso se suma una caracterización algo esquemática de sus posturas políticas y religiosas. Quiere ser película de época, drama familiar, relato de artista, thriller y tragedia, pero esa mezcla no siempre encuentra equilibrio. Adrien Brody y Guy Pearce sostienen buena parte del conjunto. Su relación mezcla dependencia, protección y amenaza con una química convincente. El apartado artístico es extraordinario, pero su irregular narrativa esta demasiado convencida de sus propias ideas.

Beautiful b-roll, excellent b-roll. Reinforced my belief that this might not be some of the most influential or the greatest cinematography and title sequences and scoring in the history of cinema, but it’s definitely some of my favourite. More overtures, more intermissions and more VistaVision please. So a lot of the same thoughts as I did the first time round. Unfortunately even in this digital age, or perhaps as a product of it, Corbet’s stylistic voice — it’s all been done before — the camerawork and editing style a dime a dozen on my social media feed, whether that’s a better produced than conceived video essay or an Instagram post shot on film in the Dolomites. Despite containing excellent sequences, and me being more receptive to the film as a whole this time around, it seriously lacks a cohesiveness, and the direction it ends up going in deflates the most intriguing elements of this premise. There’s also an enormous emptiness, a hollowness to any subtext, a chasm where substance should be present in a film that begins with fairly lofty ambitions like this one. Among what brings down this film from greatness are some strange creative decisions involving generative AI which still somewhat undermines my admiration of the film, along with the manner it sidesteps thoroughly examining its “big ideas” and central themes — whether that is Zionism or the patriarchy or capitalism or rape, your pick  — which only makes it problematic the more you think about it. Perhaps most of all it sorta squanders the fitting analogy of a struggling artist, the architect, by not fully understanding brutalism and not being comfortable enough in letting the metaphor speak for itself. As a product of being not particularly cerebral or rewarding, it fails to an extent at deconstructing biopics, displacement or even fully understanding its characters, and it really is a missed opportunity because a lot like it’s protagonist, the audience is left wondering what could’ve been. For me, too much restraint where it shouldn’t be, too much reliance on gimmickry than what should be a stronger script, and the douche bags behind this film are too far up their own ass to fix that. By the end my eyes were very sore from all the eye rolling I’d been doing across the 3.5 hr runtime… great visuals tho, and lovely music I guess.

Voto: 7.9/10 L'architettura delle cicatrici. The Brutalist si impone come un'opera monumentale e ambiziosa, un vero e proprio affresco storico che recupera il respiro del grande cinema epico del Novecento attraverso una messinscena rigorosa e di straordinaria potenza visiva. Sorretto da una fotografia che evoca la solennità dei classici, il film sfrutta ogni singolo fotogramma per costruire un'architettura visiva rigorosa, impreziosita da una colonna sonora ora minimale ora massimalista e dalle interpretazioni magistrali di Adrien Brody e Guy Pearce. Nonostante una durata imponente che richiede dedizione totale allo spettatore e una struttura narrativa a tratti debordante, il film mantiene una tensione formale altissima, dimostrando un controllo autoriale raro nel panorama contemporaneo, capace di fondere la precisione geometrica delle inquadrature con un'irrequietezza emotiva costante. Al centro di questo impianto si erge la figura complessa e tormentata di László Tóth, un architetto ebreo ungherese sopravvissuto all'Olocausto che sbarca in America carico di un talento visionario ma irrimediabilmente frammentato dal trauma. La prova di Brody è un capolavoro di sottrazione e fisicità dolente e il suo László non è il genio romantico e ispirato, ma un uomo svuotato, il cui corpo curvato dalla fatica e dagli abusi incarna letteralmente il peso di un passato indicibile. La sua psicologia è un campo di battaglia tra il furore creativo e la disperazione silenziosa, un orgoglio professionale ferito che si scontra continuamente con l'umiliazione dell'adattamento. Dall'altra parte, il magnate industriale interpretato da Guy Pearce non si limita a essere il classico antagonista capitalista, ma rappresenta una figura mefistofelica e ambigua, un mecenate paternalista e predatore che adesca l'artista non per amore dell'arte, ma per legittimare la propria autorità morale attraverso la monumentalità delle sue opere. Il rapporto simbiotico e brutale che si instaura tra i due personaggi riflette fedelmente il nucleo politico e filosofico dell'opera, configurandosi come una spietata dissezione del mito fondativo del capitalismo americano. Il talento di László viene sistematicamente mercificato, ridotto a materia prima da spremere e piegare alle esigenze di prestigio di un'élite economica che usa la cultura come vernice di facciata per celare la propria voracità. Il brutalismo stilistico ed etico che dà titolo al film non risiede soltanto nelle forme massicce del cemento a vista che l'architetto progetta, ma diventa la cifra psicologica ed esistenziale di un'intera nazione e di un'epoca, un'architettura delle cicatrici eretta sulle macerie morali dell'Occidente, dove ogni ideale di purezza estetica viene soffocato dai rapporti di forza materiali. Pur tra asperità formali e ambizioni smisurate che mettono a dura prova la resistenza dello spettatore, la pellicola lascia un segno duraturo proprio grazie a questa implacabile autopsia dei legami umani, ricordando come l'integrità di un individuo e ogni tentativo di creazione artistica nel mondo moderno siano irrimediabilmente segnati dai rapporti di forza economici, dalla violenza silenziosa e dai meccanismi predatori del potere.

I wasn't sure you could make a 2024 movie that really makes you feel like you're in the late 40s to early 60s, it's phenomenal. The movie just looks fantastic and is shot incredibly well. Secondly, the acting is phenomenal. My standout was Guy pearce, he is just so good in the movie and completely stole every scene he was in. Adrien brody is also incredible, so is Felicity jones. Just a great cast overall, and the intro credits were especially phenomenal. The story itself is interesting. It plays so much like a biopic that I was completely convinced Lazlo toth was a real person until I found out he wasn't after the movie ended, which was honestly a disappointment since I was hoping I'd be learning about a real architect and the beginnings of brutalist architecture. But even then, I love architecture, so I enjoyed watching it. What really works is how the movie explores post-war life, immigration, exploitation and the compromises people make in pursuit of success. Though after it ended, I honestly started questioning whether this was really worthy of such an epic runtime and scale because the story is ultimately a lot more intimate than it initially appears. Given how little happens in the grand scheme of things, maybe 3 hours 20 minutes wasn't necessary, even if I never felt bored during it. It just didn't lead to as much as I expected. Though I have to say, I was really surprised by the pacing. I was expecting to fall asleep halfway through given the movie's epic length, slow-burn storytelling and the fact that I started it near midnight. Yet somehow it never felt like a bore or a drag. If anything, it completely extinguished my sleepiness as it went on. I wasn't too fond of how the movie handled zionism, the repeated tiptoeing around the subject throughout the film, especially with the 'formation of Israel' montage and the implication of aliyah at the end as the answer to the failed American dream, felt a bit too neat and uncritical without considering more than 1 side to the problem. Understandable as a product of the culture, characters, period and historical context, but I still didn't appreciate how those ideas were presented in final. Besides that, it's a pretty unique movie overall, one you wouldn't expect to release during recent times. And its extremely impressive that this was made on a sub 10 million budget. That's honestly shocking. The scale of the production, the Vistavision photography, the period recreation and overall craftsmanship make it feel far more expensive than it actually was. So yeah, beautifully made film, incredibly acted and consistently engaging throughout. Just not fully convinced that the story itself justifies the epic runtime and scale it demands.

Cinema and Architecture in a Single Film? Yes. The Brutalist definitely brings together my two greatest passions to present an extremely dense drama about pain, desire, obsession, and deep trauma, expressed through an art form as abstract as architectural design. The details and finishing touches, the straight lines, the play of light, and the raw concrete masterfully convey the pain of an artist destroyed by war, broken by a foreign country, and obsessed with a work that, in reality, belongs to someone else. I suppose The Brutalist is one of those extremely difficult films to watch. Nearly three and a half hours of runtime will scare many people away, and its slow, methodical, subtext-heavy plot will drive away whatever few have decided to stay. But if one has enough patience and openness to let themselves be absorbed by the generational drama presented by the film, The Brutalist will fly by and eventually become a masterful study, not only of a character, but of an entire generation forced to carry on with their lives in a postwar period almost as unreal as the war itself. People as privileged as László Tóth can express that uncertainty, that fear, that anger, and even their darkest desires through a building almost as monumental as it is exorbitant. Others, on the other hand, are forced to self-destruct through drugs, sexual violence, and a love relationship strong enough to survive a war, but incapable of enduring its aftermath. No. The Brutalist is not for everyone. And I will not say that it is perfect either. But it is precisely what it needs to be to become a cinematic landmark: living proof that many of us are willing to endure a slow and meditative story in order to reach a thesis that is powerful, devastating, and, above all, honest. By the way, Brutalism is an architectural movement hated by many because of its simplicity and, as its name suggests, its sordid brutality. To me, however, it is the most beautiful style in architecture. Even with its simplicity, the rawness of its materials, and its violent forms, it manages to achieve a pure kind of beauty without the need for ornamentation or retouching. Almost in the same way we humans are made. 4.5 out of 5

“Is there a better description of a cube than that of its construction?” The Brutalist is an ambitious, visually stunning epic about art, ambition, trauma, and the complicated price of the American Dream. Brady Corbet creates a film that feels deliberately monumental, mirroring its main character’s obsession with architecture through its enormous scale and imposing visual language. Adrien Brody gives a remarkable performance as László Tóth , a Hungarian-Jewish architect rebuilding his life in post-war America. His character is deeply flawed, and often difficult to understand, but Brody gives him a quiet intensity that makes his struggles compelling. Felicity Jones and Guy Pearce are equally strong, adding layers to the film’s complicated relationships and power dynamics. The architecture is arguably the film’s greatest achievement. The brutalist structures are cold, imposing, and beautiful, functioning almost like another character. The cinematography and Daniel Blumberg’s haunting score give the film a weight that makes even its quieter moments feel significant. At nearly four hours, however, The Brutalist can feel a little prolonged. Some scenes linger longer than necessary, and its deliberately slow pace demands patience. The film also occasionally leans so heavily into its symbolism and grandeur that its emotional impact becomes slightly less immediate. Still, these aren’t huge criticisms. The Brutalist is the kind of film that feels increasingly rare now: visually bold, and genuinely interested in exploring difficult ideas rather than simply telling a straightforward story. It won’t work for everyone, but for viewers willing to surrender to its pace and scale, it is an unforgettable cinematic experience. This continues to be my comfort film, one I have watched now 5-6 times since I first saw it over a year and a half ago. I wanted so desperately to understand The Brutalist, what is was trying to say, but perhaps Zsofia’s message at the Venice Biennale is the most poignant “it says nothing, it conveys nothing, it just is”. Laszlo Toth (Adrien Brody) is all of us, and completely unrecognizable at the same time. It’s his genius that inspires us to reach for a better life, and that betrays his patron, Harrison Van Buren (Guy Pearce) against him. The Brutalist gives true credence to the immigrant experience in America, inspired by other masterful works, from Welles’ The Magnificent Ambersons to Coppola’s Godfather to Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut. The Brutalist fundamentally asks, who gets to be an American? Who gets to be remembered? We can thank Laszlo and Erserbet (Felicity Jones) for choosing not to answer either question. There are two distinct moments in the film that I feel my dad’s presence-in its beginning, when Laszlo arrives in America in 1947, as Daniel Blumberg’s piano fades over the skyline at the Battery, with the Woolworth building in the background. A view I got used to when I grew up, without the Towers, as my dad would take my brother and I to the park to play catch. The next is at the end, on the gondola, as Laszlo makes his way to the Biennale. Museums were my dad’s favorite place to take us, from MoMa PS1 to The Fricke and so on…The Biennale in Venice was the only place that as a child, I felt free to roam, to explore the art without being confronted by it. To dream. I believe this is the vision Laszlo had for his own constructions-brutalist in design, reminiscent of Buchenwald and Dachau, but left with enough light coming through the ceiling to promise its inhabitants of life’s natural beauty. That wandering eye is something my father understood, and a quality I wrestle with every day. On this slow, steady day, I choose to remember my dad by rewatching one of my favorite films of all time, The Brutalist.

La sensation d’après-guerre et des traumatismes qui se retransmettent par la création artistique, c’est du génie. Globalement, on observe à quel point un talent peut être gâché par l’ensemble de son environnement. La folie ne vient pas soudainement, c’est lent, calculé : puis un craquage brutal. Et franchement l’imperfection du personnage principal fait la beauté du film ; dire qu’il plonge même ceux qui l’entourent dans sa destruction c’est fou ! Les rebondissements désespèrent par les traumatismes qu’ils laissent et il faut laisser du temps à l’intrigue pour qu’ils remontent à la surface.
